items.title: Cell attachment by a characteristic map
items.strategy: Define the adjunction-space quotient X union_f D^n, including the n=0 convention S^{-1}=empty, and name its characteristic map and open cell.

items.title: The interior of an attached cell embeds openly in its closure
items.strategy: Use the quotient relation to show no interior points are identified, then distinguish the embedded open cell from the possibly nonembedded closed-cell image.

items.title: CW complex with closure finiteness and weak topology
items.strategy: Define a CW decomposition through characteristic cells, closure finiteness, and the weak topology tested on closed-cell closures; neither clause is suppressed for infinite complexes.

items.title: Skeleta, CW subcomplexes, and relative CW complexes
items.strategy: Define skeleta and require a CW subcomplex to contain the entire closure of every open cell it contains; define relative CW attachment from that subcomplex.

items.title: CW skeleta are closed and cells form a disjoint partition
items.strategy: Test each skeleton on every characteristic disk, using induction on cell dimension for the boundary preimage, then use the open-cell partition for the skeletal difference.

items.title: A compact subspace of a CW complex meets only finitely many cells
items.strategy: If infinitely many cells are met, use closure finiteness and the weak topology to construct an open cover of the compact set with no finite subcover.

items.title: The image of a compact space lies in a finite CW subcomplex
items.strategy: Take the finitely many cells meeting the image and their finitely many closure faces to form the required finite subcomplex.

items.title: Relative CW inclusions are cofibrations
items.strategy: Extend a prescribed homotopy one attached disk at a time and use the weak topology to assemble the extensions, giving the homotopy extension property.

items.title: A CW complex is the colimit of its skeleta in the weak topology
items.strategy: Translate the weak-topology clause from closed-cell closures to skeleta and prove the stated continuity criterion.

items.title: Relative homology of consecutive CW skeleta
items.strategy: Collapse the lower skeleton to a wedge of spheres, use compact-image finite-cell support to obtain a direct sum for an infinite wedge, and treat n=0 and the empty-cell case separately.

items.title: Oriented cellular chain group
items.strategy: Define C_n^cell(X;G)=H_n(X^n,X^(n-1);G) and fix generators from orientations of characteristic disks.

items.title: Cellular boundary from three consecutive skeleta
items.strategy: Define d_n as the triple connecting map followed by the relative quotient map, with one displayed sign convention.

items.title: The cellular boundary squares to zero
items.strategy: Read two consecutive connecting-and-quotient composites in the exact triple-of-skeleta diagram; exactness makes their composite zero.

items.title: Cellular homology
items.strategy: Define cellular homology as the homology of the completed cellular chain complex, with zero groups in negative degrees.

items.title: Skeletal homology stabilizes away from the cell dimension
items.strategy: Use the long exact sequence of (X^(n+1),X^n) and the concentration of its relative homology in degree n+1.

items.title: Homology of an infinite CW complex is the colimit of skeletal homology
items.strategy: Place each finite singular cycle and bounding chain in a finite subcomplex, proving both surjectivity and injectivity of the skeletal colimit map.

items.title: Cellular homology computes singular homology
items.strategy: Identify cycles and boundaries in the stable skeletal exact sequences with kernels and images of d, then use the finite-support colimit lemma for the infinite-dimensional case.

items.title: Relative cellular homology computes relative singular homology
items.strategy: For nonempty A pass to the quotient CW complex X/A, identify the reduced cellular complex with the quotient cellular complex, and use the good-pair quotient theorem; handle empty A by the absolute theorem.

items.title: Incidence number of two CW cells
items.strategy: Use the quotient degree for n at least two and define the n=1 coefficient separately as terminal-vertex multiplicity minus initial-vertex multiplicity.

items.title: Cellular boundary is the incidence degree matrix
items.strategy: Project the triple connecting map to each cell summand, use quotient degrees in dimensions at least two and the endpoint boundary in dimension one, and sum the coefficients.

items.title: Cellular maps induce cellular chain maps
items.strategy: Use a map preserving skeleta to obtain compatible maps of relative groups, then commute the triple connectors to prove the chain-map relation and singular compatibility.

items.title: A CW complex with no cells in adjacent dimensions has zero cellular boundary
items.strategy: For every degree, either the source or target cellular group is zero, so every differential vanishes and the displayed homology follows.

items.title: Euler characteristic of a finite CW complex
items.strategy: Define chi(X) as the alternating sum of the finite cell counts and state the finite-CW qualification explicitly.

items.title: Euler–Poincare formula for finite CW complexes
items.strategy: Apply rank-nullity to the finite free cellular complex so boundary ranks cancel in the alternating sum, then transfer from cellular to singular homology.

items.title: Euler characteristic is additive for finite CW pairs
items.strategy: Partition the cells of X into those of the finite subcomplex A and those outside it, then account for the quotient basepoint convention.

items.title: Euler characteristic of a finite CW product
items.strategy: Use product cells indexed by pairs of cells and factor the finite double alternating sum into the product of the two Euler characteristics.

title: Cw Complexes and Cellular Homology — Examples

items.title: Cellular homology of real projective space
items.strategy: Use the one-cell-per-dimension structure and the incidence number 1+(-1)^n, then compute kernels and images including the zero-dimensional and top-dimensional cases.

items.title: Cellular homology and ring-independent groups of complex projective space
items.strategy: Use the single even-dimensional cell in each degree to compute the additive groups over the stated coefficient ring without asserting the future cup-product structure.

items.title: Cellular boundary matrix of a closed orientable surface
items.strategy: Abelianize the standard polygon attaching word, show each one-cell coefficient cancels, and calculate the resulting integral homology.

items.title: Cellular homology of a lens space
items.strategy: Write the four-term cellular complex of the standard lens-space CW structure and isolate the multiplication-by-p differential that produces torsion.

items.title: Cellular homology of an infinite-dimensional projective space
items.strategy: Compute in finite projective skeleta in each fixed degree and pass to the colimit, keeping the infinite-dimensional justification visible.

items.title: Two CW structures on the circle have the same Euler characteristic
items.strategy: Compare the one-vertex/one-edge and subdivided structures directly, then identify their common value with the homological formula.

items.title: The closure of a CW cell need not be a closed ball
items.strategy: Attach one 1-cell to one 0-cell with both boundary points identified and distinguish its quotient closure from a closed interval.

items.title: A cell decomposition without the weak topology need not be a CW complex
items.strategy: Give the source-standard infinite-wedge variant with a strictly finer ambient topology, and exhibit the set whose cellwise tests pass while ambient closure fails.

items.title: The Hawaiian earring is not a CW complex with its punctured circles as cells
items.strategy: Treat each punctured circle as the proposed open one-cell and use compactness plus the finite-cell-intersection lemma to contradict the CW property.
